title: Does the Othello-GPT Linear World Model Replicate in a Connect-Four Transformer?

original_idea.body:
# Does the Othello-GPT Linear World Model Replicate in a Connect-Four Transformer?

**Problem:** Nanda showed Othello-GPT linearly encodes board state as 'mine vs theirs' rather than 'black vs white,' and the probe is causally usable. It is unknown whether a linear emergent world model arises with the same 'relative-to-current-player' coordinate trick in a structurally different game like Connect Four, where gravity constrains moves and the board is rectangular.

**Direction:** Train a tiny GPT (1-2 layers, available training scripts run in under an hour on a consumer GPU) on legal Connect-Four move sequences, then fit linear probes for cell occupancy under both 'absolute color' and 'relative-to-mover' encodings. Replicate Nanda's finding by testing which coordinate system yields a clean linear probe, and do a causal intervention by editing the probed direction to flip a cell and checking legal-move predictions.

**Why it matters:** World-model extraction from neural networks is a flagged open problem (Alignment Forum agenda). Confirming whether the 'relative coordinate' linear-representation trick is a general property of game transformers or an Othello quirk informs whether interpretability methods will generalize to the world models inside real agents — work fully doable outside a lab on toy models.

**Relevant context:** Nanda 2023 'Actually, Othello-GPT Has A Linear Emergent World Representation' showed board state is linearly probeable under a 'mine/theirs' (relative to current player) encoding and is causally editable. Linear Latent World Models (arXiv:2310.07582) confirmed causal utility. Chess emergent world models (arXiv:2403.15498) extended this to chess.

title: Logit Lens Failure Modes Replicated on Instruction-Tuned vs Base Models

# Logit Lens Failure Modes Replicated on Instruction-Tuned vs Base Models

**Problem:** The tuned-lens paper noted the simple logit lens is brittle and 'fails on many modern architectures,' motivating learnable translators. But the comparison was mostly base models. It is unclear whether instruction tuning makes the raw logit lens more or less reliable than on the corresponding base model — a question relevant to whether cheap interpretability shortcuts survive RLHF-style tuning.

**Direction:** Take paired base and instruction-tuned checkpoints (Pythia base vs an instruction-tuned variant, Llama-3.2-1B vs -1B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2b vs -2b-it). Apply the plain logit lens at every layer and measure per-layer KL divergence to the final distribution and top-1 agreement. Replicate the tuned-lens 'logit lens is brittle' finding, then add the twist of quantifying how the brittleness changes after instruction tuning within each family.

**Why it matters:** Logit lens is the cheapest interpretability probe and is widely used for monitoring intermediate model 'beliefs.' Knowing whether safety-relevant tuning silently degrades the reliability of this monitor — using only public checkpoints and a single GPU — directly informs whether such lightweight monitors can be trusted on deployed (tuned) models.

**Relevant context:** Belrose et al. 2023 'Eliciting Latent Predictions with the Tuned Lens' (arXiv:2303.08112) showed the logit lens is brittle and biased while the tuned lens works across Pythia, GPT-NeoX, BLOOM, GPT-Neo, OPT. 'interpreting GPT: the logit lens' (LessWrong) is the original technique.

title: Replicating the Induction-Head Phase Change on Non-Language Token Streams

# Replicating the Induction-Head Phase Change on Non-Language Token Streams

**Problem:** Induction heads emerge during a sharp phase change in 2-layer transformers trained on language, marking the onset of in-context learning. It is unknown whether the same phase-change signature appears when the same tiny architecture is trained on a structurally different, non-linguistic repeated-token stream (e.g., synthetic DNA-like sequences or MIDI note tokens), or whether language statistics are needed.

**Direction:** Use the TransformerLens 'Induction Heads Phase Change Replication' as the baseline, training a 2-layer attention-only transformer. The twist: swap the training corpus for a synthetic non-language sequence dataset with controllable repeat structure, and measure whether the loss bump and induction-head formation co-occur. Compare the timing and sharpness of the phase change to the language baseline.

**Why it matters:** Induction heads are a canonical interpretability circuit and a model of how in-context learning (and thus prompt-based capability elicitation) arises. Understanding whether the circuit's emergence is corpus-dependent helps predict when ICL-driven capabilities appear in models trained on novel data types — a controlled, lab-free training-dynamics study scoped to a tiny model.

**Relevant context:** Olsson et al. 2022 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads' (arXiv:2209.11895, transformer-circuits.pub) established the induction-head phase change and loss bump in 2-layer models. TransformerLens ships an 'Induction Heads Phase Change Replication' demo.

# Benchmark Saturation Check: Do Modern Small Models Trivially Pass Old Jailbreak Sets?

**Problem:** Many jailbreak benchmarks were built against older models. If current small open models trivially refuse the canonical attack sets, those benchmarks no longer discriminate — yet they are still widely cited, an unaddressed measurement issue.

**Direction:** Run a panel of small open models (2024 vs 2026 releases) against a fixed legacy jailbreak set and StrongREJECT, measuring attack-success distributions. Quantify ceiling/floor effects and item-level discrimination (which prompts still separate models from each other vs which everything now refuses). Recommend a discriminating subset.

**Why it matters:** Prevents the field from reporting reassuring numbers on saturated benchmarks. A pure measurement-validity contribution, lab-independent, that helps keep adversarial-robustness evaluation honest as models improve.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) was itself created because prior benchmarks overstated jailbreak success, establishing that benchmark validity erodes over time. Context file lists multiple benchmarks (AILuminate, HELM Safety, StrongReject, TrustLLM) whose discrimination on current models is untested.

title: Re-running the 'Do I Know This Entity?' Hallucination Circuit on a Different Model Family
quick_reasoning: Targets the specific hallucination/refusal-gating circuit with a focused cross-family causal replication, safety relevance obvious.

original_idea.body:
# Re-running the 'Do I Know This Entity?' Hallucination Circuit on a Different Model Family

**Problem:** Ferrando et al. found 'entity recognition' SAE latents in Gemma-2-2b that gate a default refusal/hallucination response (peaking at layer 9), partially replicated on Llama-3.1-8B. Whether the same known-entity gating mechanism exists in an architecturally distinct small family like Qwen2.5 or Phi, using their respective public SAEs/probes, remains untested.

**Direction:** Replicate the core causal result with a linear probe approach: build known/unknown entity prompt sets, train layer-wise linear probes for 'model knows this entity,' find the layer where probe accuracy peaks, and steer along the probe direction to test whether it induces hallucination (on known entities) or refusal (on unknown). The twist: run on Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B where no published entity-circuit analysis exists, comparing the peak layer and steering strength to Gemma's layer-9 result.

**Why it matters:** A model 'knowing what it knows' is the mechanistic basis of calibrated refusal and hallucination avoidance — a fuzzy, hard-to-evaluate safety property. Showing whether this circuit is family-universal, using only public weights and probes on one GPU, advances whether hallucination-monitoring directions transfer across the open models a deployer might choose.

**Relevant context:** Ferrando et al. ICLR 2025 'Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations' (arXiv:2411.14257) found entity-recognition SAE latents peaking at Gemma-2-2b layer 9 that causally gate refusal/hallucination, replicated on Llama-3.1-8B via LlamaScope SAEs.

title: Replicating Truth-Probe Generalization Failures on a New Topic Domain
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped test of truth-probe (lie-detection) generalization, a specific safety-monitoring reliability problem.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Truth-Probe Generalization Failures on a New Topic Domain

**Problem:** Truth probes trained on factual statements often fail to generalize, and recent work shows truthfulness representations rely on 'superficial resemblance.' Most studies use general-knowledge or city/geography datasets. Whether the brittleness replicates — and how it changes — when probes are trained on one knowledge domain (e.g., biology facts) and tested on a structurally different domain (e.g., legal/historical facts) is underexplored at small scale.

**Direction:** Replicate the Geometry-of-Truth probing setup on Gemma-2-2b/Llama-3.2-3B: train a linear truth probe on true/false statements from one domain and evaluate cross-domain transfer. The twist: systematically vary surface form (negation, paraphrase, language) within and across domains to test the 'superficial resemblance' hypothesis, reporting where the probe's accuracy collapses.

**Why it matters:** Lie/deception detection via internal truth directions is a leading lab-free safety tool, but its reliability hinges on generalization. Mapping exactly which distribution shifts break a truth probe — with public datasets and a single GPU — directly tells safety practitioners how far they can trust these monitors, a >1-year-horizon concern frontier labs underinvest in.

**Relevant context:** Marks & Tegmark 'The Geometry of Truth' established linear truth probes; 'How well do truth probes generalise?' (LessWrong) documented transfer failures; 'LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance' (arXiv:2510.11905) and 'Probing the Geometry of Truth' (arXiv:2506.00823) show brittleness under logical transformations.

title: Vision-SAE Low-Sparsity Result Replicated on Medical/Satellite Image Domains
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted at multimodal interpretability transfer to high-stakes domains, reasonably scoped with public SAEs.

original_idea.body:
# Vision-SAE Low-Sparsity Result Replicated on Medical/Satellite Image Domains

**Problem:** ViT-Prisma reported the surprising result that effective vision SAEs need substantially lower sparsity than language SAEs, and reconstructions can even decrease model loss. This was characterized on natural-image CLIP/DINO. Whether the low-sparsity property holds when the underlying images come from a very different distribution (medical scans, satellite imagery) — where features may be denser or rarer — is unknown.

**Direction:** Take Prisma's 80+ pre-trained CLIP SAE weights and run inference on a domain-shifted image set (e.g., a public chest X-ray or satellite-tile dataset). Replicate the sparsity-pattern measurement (L0, fraction of dead features, reconstruction effect on loss) and compare to natural-image baselines. The twist: characterize how SAE sparsity and feature firing change under domain shift without any retraining.

**Why it matters:** Multimodal interpretability is a named open problem, and vision models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains (medicine, surveillance) outside frontier labs. Understanding whether pre-trained interpretability tooling transfers to these domains, using only public SAE weights and one GPU, is exactly the kind of lab-independent, application-relevant work that scales interpretability to real deployments.

**Relevant context:** Prisma toolkit (arXiv:2504.19475) ships 80+ pre-trained CLIP/DINO SAEs and reports vision SAEs exhibit substantially lower sparsity than language SAEs, with reconstructions sometimes decreasing model loss. 'Interpretable and Testable Vision Features via SAEs' (arXiv:2502.06755) provides feature-interpretation methods.

title: Replicating Grokking Progress Measures on a Non-Modular Algorithmic Task
quick_reasoning: Studies grokking/training-dynamics interpretability, a recognized open problem, with a focused algorithmic-task replication.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Grokking Progress Measures on a Non-Modular Algorithmic Task

**Problem:** Nanda et al. reverse-engineered the Fourier-multiplication algorithm behind grokked modular addition and defined progress measures showing memorization, circuit-formation, and cleanup phases. They replicated on a few tasks. Whether the same three-phase signature and a clean interpretable circuit emerge for a non-arithmetic task like sorting short lists or computing parity is a fresh test of generality.

**Direction:** Reuse the public grokking training code to train a 1-layer transformer on a small algorithmic task that is NOT modular arithmetic (e.g., list parity or comparison). Replicate the restricted-loss / excluded-loss progress measures to detect the three training phases. The twist: attempt to reverse-engineer the learned circuit and report whether it is as cleanly interpretable as the Fourier algorithm, or whether grokking yields a messier mechanism.

**Why it matters:** Training dynamics shaping learned features is a flagged open problem. Grokking is a clean lab-free testbed for studying how and when models switch from memorization to generalization — a mechanism behind sudden capability jumps. Testing whether the interpretability story generalizes beyond arithmetic informs whether we can predict and interpret emergent generalization in general.

**Relevant context:** Nanda et al. ICLR 2023 'Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability' (arXiv:2301.05217) reverse-engineered the DFT-based modular-addition algorithm, defined restricted/excluded-loss progress measures, and identified memorization, circuit-formation, and cleanup phases; replicated on several algorithmic tasks.

title: SAE Seed-Dependence Replicated on Vision Transformers
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reproducibility check on SAE feature stability, directly bearing on trust in interpretability for safety.

original_idea.body:
# SAE Seed-Dependence Replicated on Vision Transformers

**Problem:** Recent work shows SAEs trained on the same LLM data with different random seeds learn substantially different features (only ~30% shared in a Llama-3-8B FFN SAE), with TopK SAEs more seed-dependent than ReLU. This instability has only been studied in language SAEs. Whether vision SAEs (ViT-Prisma) suffer the same seed-dependence — or are more stable because of their denser features — is unknown.

**Direction:** Train multiple small CLIP-layer SAEs from different seeds using Prisma/SAELens on a fixed activation cache (trainable in a few hours on one GPU). Replicate the seed-overlap analysis: measure the fraction of features shared across seeds via maximum cosine-similarity matching, separately for ReLU and TopK. The twist: compare the seed-stability of vision SAEs to the published language numbers, testing whether vision's lower sparsity yields more reproducible features.

**Why it matters:** If SAE features are seed-dependent, any safety claim built on 'we found feature X' is suspect unless it survives across initializations. Establishing whether this reproducibility problem extends to vision — a fully open, single-GPU study — directly bears on how much trust to place in feature-based interpretability for safety, the kind of methodological rigor labs rarely prioritize.

**Relevant context:** 'SAEs Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features' (arXiv:2501.16615) found only ~30% feature overlap across seeds in Llama-3-8B, with TopK more seed-dependent than ReLU. 'Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces' (arXiv:2606.12138) refines this. Prisma/SAELens enable vision SAE training.

title: Replicating the Poetry Planning-Ahead Circuit in Open Models with Circuit Tracing
quick_reasoning: Targets forward-planning circuits near deceptive-planning threat models with a focused circuit-tracing replication.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the Poetry Planning-Ahead Circuit in Open Models with Circuit Tracing

**Problem:** Anthropic found Claude 3.5 Haiku 'plans ahead' when writing rhyming poetry — activating the rhyme word before composing the line. Their open-source circuit-tracing tools support Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b, but it is unknown whether these much smaller open models exhibit any detectable forward-planning for rhyme, or whether planning is a capability that only appears at larger scale.

**Direction:** Use the open-source circuit-tracing library (attribution graphs via cross-layer transcoders) on Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b. Prompt for rhyming couplets and look for activations corresponding to the eventual rhyme word appearing before the line is written, replicating Anthropic's methodology on a couplet dataset. The twist: compare the two small models to test whether planning-ahead correlates with capability/scale even within the small regime.

**Why it matters:** Forward planning (representing a future goal before acting) is mechanistically close to the hidden-goal and deceptive-planning threat models that matter for long-horizon safety. Detecting whether and at what scale planning circuits appear, using only open tools and small models on one GPU, is a tractable slice of a >1-year threat model and tests interpretability's reach into model 'intent.'

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2025 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' and 'Circuit Tracing' (transformer-circuits.pub) found Claude 3.5 Haiku activates rhyme words before writing the line. Anthropic open-sourced circuit-tracing tools (cross-layer transcoders, attribution graphs) supporting Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b, with a Neuronpedia frontend.

title: Re-deriving Steering Vectors Across Quantization Levels
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped deployment-reality check on whether steering/safety tooling survives quantization, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Re-deriving Steering Vectors Across Quantization Levels

**Problem:** Activation-addition steering vectors (e.g., refusal, sentiment, sycophancy directions) are extracted from full-precision activations. Hobbyists almost always run quantized models (4-bit, 8-bit) on consumer GPUs. Whether steering vectors extracted at full precision still steer effectively when applied to the quantized version of the same model — and whether vectors extracted from the quantized model differ — is largely untested.

**Direction:** Pick one well-studied steering direction (e.g., the refusal or a sentiment direction) on a small open model. Replicate the difference-of-means extraction and steering-effect measurement at full precision (baseline). The twist: apply the same vector to the 4-bit and 8-bit quantized model, and separately extract vectors from the quantized activations, comparing steering efficacy and direction cosine-similarity across precisions.

**Why it matters:** Almost all real-world local deployment of open models is quantized, yet interpretability and steering research is done at full precision. Checking whether mechanistic interventions survive quantization — a cheap single-GPU study — tells us whether safety tooling (and conversely, jailbreak steering) transfers to the models people actually run, a deployment-reality gap labs ignore.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. (arXiv:2406.11717) and the broader representation-engineering literature (arXiv:2502.17601) extract steering directions via difference-of-means at full precision. TransformerLens supports activation extraction; bitsandbytes enables 4/8-bit quantized inference on consumer GPUs.

title: Replicating Multilingual Circuit Findings on Low-Resource Languages
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted at cross-lingual safety gaps via interpretability, reasonably scoped on low-resource languages.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Multilingual Circuit Findings on Low-Resource Languages

**Problem:** Anthropic's circuit tracing showed multilingual representations share language-agnostic features in Claude 3.5 Haiku, and the open tools were demoed on multilingual tasks in Gemma-2-2b. These analyses focused on high-resource languages (English, French, Chinese). Whether the shared-concept 'lingua franca' representation extends to low-resource languages — or whether such languages route through English — is open.

**Direction:** Use the logit lens / tuned lens and simple probing on Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b for a translation-and-completion task. Replicate the finding that intermediate representations are language-agnostic by checking whether the model's intermediate predictions are English-like regardless of input language. The twist: compare a high-resource language pair to a low-resource one (e.g., Swahili, Welsh) to test whether low-resource processing detours through English.

**Why it matters:** Cross-lingual safety gaps (safety tuning failing in non-English) are a documented problem, and the mechanism likely lies in whether non-English inputs route through shared English-centric features. Mapping this for low-resource languages — using public models on one GPU — is a lab-light contribution to understanding why safety degrades multilingually, a diffuse problem labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2025 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' found shared language-agnostic features and that the model 'thinks in a conceptual space' before language; circuit-tracing tools were demoed on multilingual tasks in Gemma-2-2b. Tuned lens (arXiv:2303.08112) supports intermediate-prediction readout.

title: Feature-Universality Result Replicated Within a Single Model Family Across Scales
quick_reasoning: Precisely tests the load-bearing 'study small, deploy large' assumption via cross-scale feature universality.

original_idea.body:
# Feature-Universality Result Replicated Within a Single Model Family Across Scales

**Problem:** Work quantifying SAE feature-space universality across different LLMs found 'weak universality.' But the cleaner question — whether the SAME features (via shared SAE dictionaries on Neuronpedia) persist across model sizes within ONE family (e.g., Gemma-2-2b vs Gemma-2-9b, both with public Gemma Scope SAEs) — is more tractable and directly tests whether features are conserved as capability scales.

**Direction:** Use the public Gemma Scope SAEs for Gemma-2-2b and Gemma-2-9b. Pick a set of named, interpretable features (e.g., entity, sentiment, code) from the smaller model and find their nearest analogues in the larger model via activation correlation on shared text. Replicate the universality-quantification methodology, reporting the fraction of features with strong cross-scale matches.

**Why it matters:** If features are conserved across scale within a family, interpretability and safety findings on small models transfer to large ones — a load-bearing assumption for the entire 'study small, deploy large' research strategy. Testing this with public SAEs on one GPU directly validates whether cheap small-model interpretability informs frontier safety.

**Relevant context:** 'Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across LLMs via SAEs' (arXiv:2410.06981) found weak universality across models. Gemma Scope (DeepMind) provides public SAEs for all layers of Gemma-2-2b and -9b; Neuronpedia hosts feature dashboards and an API.

title: Replicating Activation Patching for IOI on a Non-English Indirect-Object Task
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted at cross-lingual circuit reuse bearing on language-switch safety bypasses, focused IOI replication.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Activation Patching for IOI on a Non-English Indirect-Object Task

**Problem:** The Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small is the canonical activation-patching case study, fully reverse-engineered with name-mover and S-inhibition heads. It is unknown whether the same circuit structure is reused when the identical grammatical task is posed in another language, or whether the model builds a separate language-specific circuit.

**Direction:** Replicate the IOI activation-patching analysis in a small multilingual-capable model (Gemma-2-2b or a multilingual GPT-2 variant) for the standard English IOI templates, identifying the key attention heads via path patching. The twist: translate the IOI templates into a second language the model handles and re-run the patching, comparing whether the same heads carry the indirect-object signal or whether a distinct circuit appears.

**Why it matters:** Whether circuits are reused across languages bears on the cross-lingual generalization of interpretability findings and on whether safety-relevant circuits (refusal, deception) might be bypassed simply by switching language. This is a tractable, fully-open activation-patching study runnable on one GPU, extending a textbook result in a fresh direction.

**Relevant context:** Wang et al. 'Interpretability in the Wild: IOI in GPT-2 small' established the IOI circuit (name-mover heads, S-inhibition heads) via path patching; TransformerLens ships IOI demos and patching utilities. Multilingual representation sharing was found in Anthropic's circuit tracing.

title: Position of the Harmful Demonstration in Many-Shot Attacks
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped controlled variation isolating ordering effects in many-shot jailbreaks, a specific robustness problem.

original_idea.body:
# Position of the Harmful Demonstration in Many-Shot Attacks

**Problem:** Many-shot jailbreaking varies the number of harmful demonstrations, but not their arrangement. Whether placing the strongest harmful examples early, late, or interleaved with benign ones changes attack success at fixed shot count is an untested variation.

**Direction:** Hold shot count fixed (e.g. 64) and vary demonstration ordering: harmful-front-loaded, harmful-back-loaded, interleaved, and graded-escalation. Measure attack-success across orderings on small open long-context models, isolating recency/primacy effects in the jailbreak.

**Why it matters:** If ordering matters, defenders could disrupt many-shot attacks by shuffling or summarizing context, and the result clarifies the in-context-learning mechanism behind the attack. Cheap inference experiment on open models extending a flagship result with a new controlled variable.

**Relevant context:** Anil et al. 'Many-shot Jailbreaking' (NeurIPS 2024) characterized the power law in shot count but treated demonstrations as exchangeable; ordering is an unexamined dimension. StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) scores outcomes.

title: Tuned Lens Replicated on a State-Space (Mamba) vs Transformer Model

original_idea.body:
# Tuned Lens Replicated on a State-Space (Mamba) vs Transformer Model

**Problem:** A follow-up to the tuned lens asked whether transformer interpretability transfers to RNNs. State-space models (Mamba) are now available as small open checkpoints, but the simple question of whether logit-lens-style intermediate prediction readout works at all on a small Mamba — and how its layer-wise prediction trajectory compares to a similar-size transformer — is rarely examined hands-on.

**Direction:** Take a small open Mamba checkpoint and a similarly sized transformer. Replicate the logit-lens / tuned-lens intermediate-prediction analysis: project each layer's hidden state to vocabulary (training a small linear translator if needed) and measure per-layer KL to the final output. The twist: compare the shape of the 'prediction emerges over depth' curve between the SSM and the transformer.

**Why it matters:** Interpretability tooling is overwhelmingly transformer-centric, but alternative architectures (SSMs) are gaining adoption outside frontier labs. Testing whether basic mechanistic-readout methods transfer to a different architecture — a single-GPU study on public checkpoints — helps ensure interpretability-based safety monitoring does not silently fail when the architecture changes.

**Relevant context:** 'Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?' (arXiv:2404.05971) examined lens/probing transfer to RNN-like models. Belrose et al. tuned lens (arXiv:2303.08112) provides the readout methodology. Small Mamba checkpoints are publicly available on HuggingFace.

# Replicating SAE Feature Steering for Sentiment on a Different Modality (Audio/Code Tokens)

**Problem:** SAE feature steering (amplifying/suppressing a single interpretable latent to change behavior) is well demonstrated for text concepts like sentiment and entities in Gemma. Whether the same single-feature steering precision holds for non-prose token streams — specifically code — where the model's 'concepts' are syntactic/structural, is underexplored using public SAEs.

**Direction:** Use Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2-2b. Replicate single-feature steering on prose (e.g., steer a sentiment feature, measure effect) as the baseline. The twist: identify code-related SAE features (via Neuronpedia explanations) and test whether steering them produces clean, interpretable changes in code completions (e.g., language choice, comment density), quantifying steering precision vs side-effects relative to the prose baseline.

**Why it matters:** Code-generation models increasingly autonomously write and execute code, a key autonomy/agentic risk surface. Whether interpretable features cleanly control code behavior — testable with public SAEs on one GPU — bears on whether feature-level monitoring/steering can serve as a safety control for code agents, infrastructure valuable to build outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Gemma Scope (DeepMind) provides public SAEs for Gemma-2-2b; Neuronpedia hosts feature explanations and steering. Anthropic and Ferrando et al. (arXiv:2411.14257) demonstrate causal single-feature steering for text concepts. SAE feature steering is a standard methodology.

title: Replicating the 'Refusal Direction Survives Fine-Tuning' Question on LoRA-Tuned Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped, practically urgent test of refusal-monitor survival under LoRA fine-tuning of open models.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the 'Refusal Direction Survives Fine-Tuning' Question on LoRA-Tuned Models

**Problem:** The refusal-direction result is established on released chat models. A practically urgent variant: when a user applies a small LoRA fine-tune (the dominant cheap customization method) to an open chat model, does the original refusal direction persist, shift, or vanish? This determines whether refusal monitoring built on the base model survives community fine-tuning.

**Direction:** Extract the refusal direction from a base open chat model (difference-of-means). Apply a small, benign LoRA fine-tune on an unrelated task (runs in under an hour on one GPU). The twist: re-extract the refusal direction from the LoRA-tuned model and measure (a) cosine similarity to the original direction and (b) whether the ORIGINAL direction still ablates refusal in the tuned model.

**Why it matters:** Thousands of community LoRA fine-tunes of open models are released monthly, and many inadvertently or deliberately weaken safety. Whether a refusal monitor calibrated on the base model still works after LoRA tuning — a cheap, fully-open study — is directly relevant to monitoring the sprawling open-weights ecosystem that no single lab controls.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. (arXiv:2406.11717) found refusal is a single direction; 'Beyond Surface Alignment' (arXiv:2509.15202) studied ablating it. PEFT/LoRA fine-tuning of small models is single-GPU feasible; TransformerLens supports direction extraction on the resulting model.

title: Replicating Linear Probe 'Lie Detection' on an Open Model-Organism of Deception
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped lie-detection probe test on an instructed-deception model organism, core deceptive-alignment relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Linear Probe 'Lie Detection' on an Open Model-Organism of Deception

**Problem:** Linear probes can detect whether a model 'believes' a statement is true. But most evaluations test honest-vs-false statements, not a model actively instructed to deceive. Whether a truth probe trained on simple true/false statements transfers to detecting an instructed lie — in a small open model prompted to role-play deception — is a sharper, more safety-relevant test.

**Direction:** Train a linear truth probe on standard true/false statement activations in a small open model (Geometry-of-Truth style). The twist: construct a model-organism-style setup where the same model is prompted to knowingly assert false statements (instructed deception), and test whether the truth probe fires on the model's internal 'belief' even while the output is a lie — replicating the probing method but on deceptive rather than merely false content.

**Why it matters:** A model that says one thing while internally 'knowing' another is the core of deceptive-alignment threat models. **Problem:** ViT-Prisma found that vision SAEs show different sparsity patterns than language SAEs, but this surprising result has not been turned into a standardized set of metrics that characterize how and where vision and language SAEs differ, leaving multimodal interpretability without comparable measurements.

# Interpretability-to-Action Benchmark: Does a Feature Predict Behavior Out-of-Distribution?

**Problem:** A core open problem is the interpretability-to-safety gap: mechanistic findings rarely translate into actionable guarantees. We lack a simple benchmark asking whether a feature/probe that fires on in-distribution examples still predicts the model's behavior on out-of-distribution or adversarial inputs.

**Direction:** For a safety-relevant feature (e.g., a refusal feature/probe), measure how well its activation predicts the model's actual refusal behavior on (a) in-distribution prompts, (b) paraphrased prompts, and (c) lightly jailbroken prompts. Report the predictive-validity drop across distributions as a reusable 'actionability' score for any candidate safety feature.

**Why it matters:** A monitor that detects deception only on the prompts it was tuned on is useless against an adversary. Quantifying the OOD predictive-validity gap directly targets the interpretability-to-safety translation problem and is a measurement labs underinvest in relative to capabilities.

**Relevant context:** Bridging the interpretability-to-safety gap and developing benchmarks that test whether mechanistic findings yield actionable guarantees are explicit Open Phil/standard-priority open problems. SAEBench shows proxy metrics don't reliably translate to practical performance, motivating behavior-grounded validity tests.

# Superposition Stress Benchmark on Open Toy Models

**Problem:** Superposition (packing more features than dimensions) is a central unresolved phenomenon, but there is no easy, standardized benchmark that measures how reliably current decomposition tools recover known-ground-truth features as superposition pressure increases, in a setting where ground truth exists.

**Direction:** Build a controlled benchmark on small toy/transformer models with synthetic features at varying feature-to-dimension ratios, train (or load) small SAEs/dictionaries, and measure recovery accuracy vs. superposition ratio. Produce a 'decomposition recovery curve' tool that anyone can reuse to stress-test a decomposition method against ground truth.

**Why it matters:** Because superposition decomposition is unreliable, safety claims based on 'we decomposed the relevant features' may fail silently. A ground-truth recovery benchmark gives the field a calibration baseline and is exactly the kind of toy-model interpretability work the RFP starred, doable on a single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Understanding/decomposing superposition reliably is a flagship problem from '200 Concrete Open Problems'; Open Phil starred building toy models that capture alignment-relevant phenomena for controlled interpretability. Anthropic's Toy Models of Superposition established the synthetic-ground-truth paradigm this extends.

# Auto-Interp Robustness to Activating-Example Sampling

**Problem:** Auto-interp explanations are generated from a sampled set of a feature's top-activating examples, but the explanation (and its detection/fuzzing score) may depend heavily on which examples are sampled. This sensitivity is not standardly measured, so reported feature labels may be unstable.

**Direction:** For a set of SAE features, generate explanations multiple times from different random samples of activating examples (varying count and whether 'quantile' vs 'top' sampling) and measure explanation agreement and score variance. Produce a 'sampling robustness' metric and guidance on how many examples are needed before labels stabilize.

**Why it matters:** If a feature's interpretation flips based on a sampling artifact, downstream safety monitoring built on that label is unreliable. This is a cheap, reusable robustness check that directly improves the trustworthiness of the most-used scalable interpretability pipeline, with no lab resources required.

**Relevant context:** Delphi/Neuronpedia auto-interp pipelines select n activating examples to produce and score explanations via detection and fuzzing; sampling strategy (top vs quantile) is a known knob in EleutherAI's autointerp work. SAEBench's caution about proxy metrics motivates measuring pipeline-internal variance.

# Activation-Patching Localization Reliability Tool

**Problem:** Activation patching is the workhorse for localizing where a behavior 'lives,' but results depend on choices (corrupted-prompt construction, metric, denoising vs noising) that are rarely reported or compared. There is no standard tool that reports how stable a localization is across these methodological choices.

**Direction:** Build a wrapper around TransformerLens patching that, for a chosen task (e.g., indirect-object identification on GPT-2 small, a known circuit), runs the patch under several reasonable configurations (noising vs denoising, logit-diff vs prob metric, different corruptions) and reports a localization-stability heatmap. Surface where conclusions agree and where they're config-dependent.

**Why it matters:** Localization claims underpin much circuit-based safety reasoning; if they're brittle to defensible methodology choices, the field needs to know. A reliability tool is reusable infrastructure that raises methodological standards and is fully feasible on the well-studied IOI circuit.

**Relevant context:** Activation patching/causal tracing is a core listed methodology; the IOI circuit (Wang et al.) is a standard open benchmark task. A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability (2407.02646) catalogs patching variants (noising/denoising, metric choices) whose impact on conclusions is under-standardized.

# A 'Negative Result' Feature Registry: Concepts SAEs Fail to Capture

**Problem:** Interpretability publishing is biased toward features that were successfully found; there is no shared, structured record of safety-relevant concepts that researchers searched for in SAEs and could NOT cleanly find. This absence makes it hard to know what is genuinely hard to monitor.

**Direction:** Define a small list of safety-relevant target concepts (deception, sycophancy, situational awareness cues, refusal-evasion), then systematically search a public SAE for clean single-feature representations of each using auto-interp + targeted probes, and report which concepts have no clean feature. Publish the search protocol and a reusable template for logging negative results.

**Why it matters:** Knowing which dangerous concepts are NOT cleanly represented (and thus hard to monitor via SAEs) is as safety-relevant as knowing which are. A negative-results registry counters publication bias and is pure measurement work needing only public SAEs.

**Relevant context:** SAEBench shows feature quality/disentanglement varies widely and proxy metrics mislead; the interpretability-to-safety gap is an explicit open problem. Neuronpedia/Delphi provide the search-and-score tooling to attempt and document concept localization.

# Lens-Agreement Score: When Do Logit Lens, Tuned Lens, and Probes Tell the Same Story?

**Problem:** Multiple 'reading' tools (logit lens, tuned lens, linear probes) are used to interpret intermediate states, but they are rarely cross-validated against each other. There is no standard metric for whether these tools agree, so a conclusion may be tool-specific without anyone noticing.

**Direction:** On a few small open models, decode intermediate-layer 'next-token belief' with logit lens, a quickly trained tuned lens, and a vocabulary probe, then compute a per-layer cross-tool agreement score. Identify layers/models where tools converge (trustworthy) vs diverge (caution), and ship the agreement computation as a reusable diagnostic.

**Why it matters:** Triangulating across independent methods is the cheapest way to build calibrated trust in interpretability readouts. A standardized agreement score gives safety researchers a quick robustness signal and is entirely doable with open tooling on a consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Logit lens is unreliable in early layers (echoes input token); tuned lens (2303.08112) trains affine translators that align better with final-layer outputs. Combining lenses/probes is established practice but agreement is not standardly quantified. TransformerLens enables all three readouts.

# Feature-Splitting Diagnostic Across SAE Widths

**Problem:** As SAE width grows, a single concept can 'split' into many narrower features (feature splitting), complicating interpretation and monitoring. There is no easy tool to measure how much a given concept splits as width increases, so users can't anticipate whether their monitoring feature will fragment.

**Direction:** Using public SAEs of multiple widths trained on the same model/layer, track a fixed set of seed concepts and measure how many features each concept maps to at each width (via activation-correlation clustering + auto-interp). Produce a 'splitting curve' tool and report which safety concepts fragment fastest.

**Why it matters:** If the 'deception feature' fragments into 30 features in a wider SAE, a monitor watching one feature breaks. Quantifying feature splitting is reusable infrastructure for choosing SAE width for monitoring, requiring only public weights.

**Relevant context:** Feature splitting is documented in Anthropic's 'Towards Monosemanticity' / scaling-monosemanticity line; SAEBench released SAEs across architectures and widths enabling width sweeps. Reliable superposition decomposition is an open problem.

# Token-Depth of Safety Across Quantization Levels

**Problem:** Shallow safety alignment was measured on full-precision weights. Practitioners increasingly run 4-bit/8-bit quantized models locally, but it is unknown whether quantization erodes or shifts the first-token safety signal that alignment relies on.

**Direction:** Take one open chat model at fp16, int8, and int4 (via bitsandbytes/GGUF). Reproduce Qi et al.'s per-token KL divergence between harmful-prompt completions and a reference safe completion, plus prefilling-attack success rate at each precision. Test whether quantization disproportionately damages the shallow safety layer.

**Why it matters:** Local/edge deployment via quantization is the dominant counterfactual-to-labs use case. If quantization silently weakens shallow safety, it is a deployment-robustness gap that only outside researchers running consumer hardware would surface.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946): safety divergence concentrated in first tokens. International AI Safety Report 2026 flags lab-tested vs real-world deployment robustness gap. Quantization is a standard consumer-GPU workflow.

title: Benchmarking Auto-Interp Explanations Against Causal Effect, Not Just Activation
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped benchmark grounding auto-interp explanations in causal effect, directly improving interpretability faithfulness.

original_idea.body:
# Benchmarking Auto-Interp Explanations Against Causal Effect, Not Just Activation

**Problem:** Auto-interp scores (detection/fuzzing) measure whether an explanation predicts WHEN a feature activates, but not whether the feature CAUSES the described behavior. A feature can be correlationally interpretable yet causally inert, and there's no standard test combining the two.

**Direction:** For a sample of explained SAE features, run a cheap causal check: ablate/clamp the feature and measure whether outputs change in a way consistent with its auto-interp label. Define a combined score (correlational interpretability x causal effect) and report how often well-explained features are causally inert.

**Why it matters:** Safety monitoring wants features that causally drive behavior, not just correlate with it. A correlational-vs-causal benchmark exposes a hidden weakness of auto-interp pipelines and is reusable, lab-free measurement on public SAEs and small models.

**Relevant context:** Delphi scores explanations correlationally via detection/fuzzing. circuit-tracer validates feature roles via perturbation (feature clamping) on Gemma-2-2b/Llama-3.2-1b. SAEBench warns that proxy interpretability metrics may not reflect practical (causal) usefulness.

title: Refusal-Circuit Robustness Benchmark Under Paraphrase

original_idea.body:
# Refusal-Circuit Robustness Benchmark Under Paraphrase

**Problem:** Refusal is one of the few well-localized safety behaviors (refusal directions/features), but it's unknown how stable the localized refusal mechanism is across semantically equivalent paraphrases of harmful requests. No standard benchmark measures refusal-mechanism robustness to surface variation.

**Direction:** Construct a small set of harmful-request templates with many paraphrases, extract the refusal direction/feature in a small open model, and measure how consistently the same mechanism activates across paraphrases and how consistently ablating it removes refusal. Report a robustness score capturing paraphrase-invariance of the refusal mechanism.

**Why it matters:** If the refusal mechanism is paraphrase-fragile, jailbreaks that merely reword requests will slip past mechanism-based monitors. Measuring this is a concrete interpretability-to-safety contribution needing only open models and public refusal-direction methods.

**Relevant context:** ICLR 2025 work programs refusal with a single direction; Rogue Scalpel and SAE-steering papers manipulate refusal features but validate narrowly (single model/layer). Robustness across paraphrase is an under-measured property relevant to jailbreak defense.
